Charles Darnay. A central character in Charles Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities, a French aristocrat who renounces his title and escapes to England to forge a new identity. Though born into decadent French nobility, Darnay represents conscience and moral reform, contrasting sharply with the revolutionary fervor consuming France.

Born as Charles St. Evremonde, the nephew and heir of a wicked French marquis, he rejects the title and cruelty his family represents. His renunciation becomes an act of moral conscience. He flees France after the Revolution begins, assuming a false identity and teaching French to earn an honest living in England. His ability to reinvent himself speaks to both his resourcefulness and his isolation.

Darnay loves Lucie Manette and proposes marriage despite his secret past and uncertain future. His devotion to her is steadfast and humble, anchoring him to a vision of domestic peace. He is contrasted with Sydney Carton, the dissolute Englishman who also loves Lucie but seems unworthy of her. Darnay represents order and self-improvement where Carton represents waste and degradation.

He returns to Paris during the Terror to help his uncle's steward and is arrested. The tribunal demands blood from the St. Evremonde line, and his birth becomes his death sentence. He is saved from execution when Carton, his physical double, takes his place at the guillotine, sacrificing himself for Darnay's life and happiness with Lucie. Carton's sacrifice becomes the culmination of his wasted life. Yet Darnay embodies the individual who tries to escape history through moral action, only to discover that historical forces are indifferent to personal virtue.
